title: The Making of a Global World

learn.hook: The aloo in your samosa and the mirchi in your chutney are travellers: they came to India from the Americas only after Columbus crossed the Atlantic, a little over five centuries ago!
points: Long before modern times, travellers, traders, priests and pilgrims carried goods, money, skills, ideas and even germs across great distances.

The silk routes, named after the Chinese silk carried along them, linked Asia with Europe and northern Africa. They existed before the Christian era and thrived almost until the 15th century. Chinese pottery and textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia travelled west, while gold and silver flowed east.
Religion and culture also moved along these routes: Buddhism, which emerged in eastern India, spread in several directions through them.

Foods such as potatoes, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes reached Europe and Asia only after Christopher Columbus reached the Americas. In Ireland, poor peasants depended so much on the potato that when disease destroyed the crop in 1845 to 1849, about a million people died of starvation.

By the mid-16th century the Portuguese and Spanish conquest and colonisation of the Americas was well under way. Their most powerful weapon was not guns but germs such as smallpox, to which the local people had no immunity. Silver from mines in Peru and Mexico increased Europe's wealth. Until the 18th century, China and India were among the world's richest countries.

example.q: Think it through: Why was smallpox more powerful than weapons in the conquest of the Americas?
steps: The people of the Americas had been isolated from the rest of the world for a very long time.
So they had no immunity against diseases like smallpox carried by Europeans.
The disease spread quickly and weakened whole communities, ahead of the soldiers themselves.
This made the conquest far easier than fighting alone could have done.
example.answer: Long isolation meant the local people had no immunity to diseases like smallpox, so germs weakened communities before any battle.

learn.reallife: Next time you eat aloo paratha or tomato chutney, remember that both potatoes and tomatoes are gifts of the Americas, carried across oceans by trade.

games.title: True or false: early globalisation
items: Chillies and tomatoes were grown in India long before the Americas were reached by Columbus.
They came to Europe and Asia only after Columbus reached the Americas.
The silk routes got their name from Chinese silk carried along them.
Silk cargoes from China were among the most famous goods on these routes.
Gold and silver flowed from Europe to Asia through pre-modern trade.
Europe paid for Asian goods like spices and textiles with precious metals.
Until the 18th century, China and India were among the richest countries in the world.
They were great centres of trade and production.
The Spanish conquered the Americas mainly because their guns were better than local weapons.
Their most powerful weapon was not guns but germs such as smallpox, against which the local people had no immunity.

quiz.q: Why are the silk routes called by that name?
options: Chinese silk was one of the main goods carried along them
Silk was grown along the roads
The roads were paved with silk
Only silk was allowed on them
quiz.explain: Historians named them after the valuable Chinese silk cargoes, though many other goods also travelled on them.
quiz.mistake: Takes the name too literally

quiz.q: The silk routes linked Asia with which regions?
quiz.explain: These land and sea routes joined vast regions of Asia with Europe and northern Africa.
quiz.mistake: Includes regions not connected before modern sea voyages

quiz.q: Which religion, born in eastern India, spread in several directions along the silk routes?
quiz.explain: Buddhism emerged in eastern India and spread through the silk routes. Christian missionaries and Muslim preachers also later travelled these routes.
quiz.mistake: Does not know where the religion originated

quiz.q: Which of these foods reached India only after Columbus reached the Americas?
quiz.explain: Chillies, potatoes, tomatoes, maize and groundnuts came from the Americas. Black pepper, rice and sugarcane were grown in Asia much earlier.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all common Indian foods are native to India

quiz.q: Why did about a million people die in Ireland between 1845 and 1849?
options: A disease destroyed the potato crop on which poor peasants depended
A smallpox epidemic brought by traders
quiz.explain: Poor Irish peasants depended heavily on potatoes, so when disease destroyed the crop, famine followed.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the famine to dependence on one crop

quiz.q: What was the most powerful 'weapon' of the Spanish conquerors in the Americas?
quiz.explain: Isolated for long, the local people had no immunity against smallpox, which spread deep into the continent.
quiz.mistake: Assumes conquest was won mainly by military weapons

quiz.q: From where did silver flow to Europe after the conquest of the Americas?
quiz.explain: Silver from Peru and Mexico greatly added to Europe's wealth and financed its trade with Asia.
quiz.mistake: Does not know where the American silver came from

quiz.q: Which countries were among the richest in the world until the 18th century?
quiz.explain: China and India were pre-eminent in Asian trade until the 18th century.
quiz.mistake: Assumes Europe was always the richest region

teach.praise: Wow! Goods, foods, ideas and even germs travelled the world centuries ago!

learn.hook: In the 1800s the world got 'connected' by three flows: goods, people and money, all moving faster than ever before.
points: Economists describe three flows in the 19th-century world economy: trade (mostly in goods like cloth and wheat), labour (people migrating for work) and capital (investment over long distances).

In Britain the Corn Laws had restricted the import of corn. When they were abolished, cheaper food flowed in from places like Eastern Europe, Russia, America and Australia; British farmers could not compete, and many people moved to cities or overseas. Nearly 50 million people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia in the 19th century.

Technology such as railways, steamships and the telegraph speeded up trade, and refrigerated ships allowed meat to be carried long distances. In India, the British built canal colonies in Punjab to grow wheat and cotton for export.

In 1885 European powers met in Berlin to complete the carving up of Africa. In the late 1880s rinderpest, a cattle disease, spread through Africa and killed 90 per cent of the cattle, destroying livelihoods and forcing Africans into wage labour.

Indentured labourers from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and the dry districts of Tamil Nadu went to work in the Caribbean (Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam), Mauritius, Fiji, Ceylon and Malaya. They created new cultures such as Hosay in Trinidad and chutney music. Indentureship was abolished in 1921.

example.q: Think it through: Why did poor Indians agree to become indentured labourers?
steps: Cottage industries were declining and land rents had risen in their home regions.
Many fell into debt and could not survive on their land.
Recruiters promised jobs abroad, sometimes giving false information about the work and living conditions.
So hardship at home pushed people to accept contracts to work in faraway plantations, mines and construction sites.
example.answer: Poverty, debt and declining home industries pushed them, while recruiters' promises pulled them to distant lands.

learn.reallife: Many people of Indian origin in Fiji, Mauritius, Trinidad and Guyana are descendants of indentured labourers, and some still celebrate Diwali and sing Bhojpuri songs there.

items.text: Britain's ___ Laws restricted the import of corn.

quiz.q: Which three flows did economists identify in the 19th-century world economy?
quiz.explain: Trade in goods, migration of labour and movement of capital for investment were the three flows that knitted economies together.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the flows with the technologies that helped them

quiz.q: What happened after the Corn Laws were abolished in Britain?
options: Corn prices in Britain rose sharply
Cheaper food was imported and British agriculture could not compete
British farmers began exporting corn to India
quiz.explain: Food could now be imported more cheaply than it was grown in Britain, so large areas went uncultivated and people left for cities or overseas.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the effect of removing import restrictions

quiz.q: About how many people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia in the 19th century?
quiz.explain: Nearly 50 million Europeans left for America and Australia, looking for land and work.
quiz.mistake: Has no sense of the scale of migration

quiz.q: Why did the British build canal colonies in Punjab?
options: To stop indentured labourers from leaving
To supply drinking water to London
To turn semi-desert land into fertile land for growing wheat and cotton for export
quiz.explain: Canals irrigated semi-desert wastes so that Punjab could grow export crops like wheat and cotton.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect canal colonies with export agriculture

quiz.q: What was the main purpose of the Berlin conference of 1885?
options: European powers met to complete the carving up of Africa
To end the First World War
quiz.explain: At Berlin in 1885 the big European powers divided African territory among themselves.
quiz.mistake: Confuses this meeting with other conferences in the syllabus

quiz.q: What was rinderpest?
options: A fast-spreading cattle disease that killed most of Africa's cattle
A crop disease that destroyed potatoes in Ireland
quiz.explain: Rinderpest arrived in Africa in the late 1880s and killed 90 per cent of the cattle, destroying African livelihoods.
quiz.mistake: Confuses rinderpest with the Irish potato blight

quiz.q: Who was an indentured labourer?
options: A soldier recruited for the British army
A free worker who could change jobs at any time
A bonded labourer under contract to work for an employer for a fixed period
A trader who lent money to farmers
quiz.explain: Indentured labourers signed contracts to work for a specific time, often to pay for their passage, and could not leave freely.
quiz.mistake: Thinks indentured labour was free wage labour

quiz.q: In which year was indentured labour from India abolished?
quiz.explain: Indian nationalist leaders opposed it as a new system of slavery, and it was abolished in 1921.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the year with other dates from the chapter

teach.praise: Excellent! Trade, people and money flowed together, but not always fairly.
teach.nudge: Can you name the three flows, and tell me what indentured labour was?

topics.title: The inter-war economy and the Great Depression

learn.hook: One terrible war, one car factory in Detroit and one big economic crash: the years 1914 to the 1930s changed the world economy.
points: The First World War (1914 to 1918) was fought between the Allies (Britain, France and Russia, later joined by the US) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey). It was the first modern industrial war, using machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons.

Britain borrowed large sums from US banks and the US public, so the US turned from an international debtor into an international creditor. After the war, Britain faced huge debts and unemployment, and lost much of its Indian cotton market to Japan.

In the US, Henry Ford adapted the assembly line to car-making in Detroit and produced the T-Model Ford. In January 1914 he raised the daily wage of his workers to $5, roughly double the earlier wage. Mass production lowered costs, and hire purchase let people buy on credit.

The Great Depression began around 1929 and lasted till the mid-1930s. Agricultural overproduction made prices fall, and when the US cut back its overseas loans, many countries faced crisis. In the US, between 1929 and 1932 about 110,000 companies collapsed.

In India, between 1928 and 1934 exports and imports nearly halved and wheat prices fell by 50 per cent. Peasants could not pay revenue and fell into debt, and India exported precious metals, notably gold.

example.q: Think it through: Why did Indian peasants suffer badly in the Great Depression even though prices fell?
steps: Peasants sold crops in the market, so falling prices cut their incomes sharply.
But the colonial government did not reduce revenue demands.
So peasants had to pay the same tax out of much smaller earnings.
Many used up savings, mortgaged land or sold gold and silver jewellery to survive.
example.answer: Their crop prices and incomes fell, but revenue demands did not, so they fell into debt and sold land and jewellery.

learn.reallife: When people buy a phone or a scooter on EMIs today, they are using credit, much like the hire purchase that spread in 1920s America.

games.title: Who or what?
pairs: Britain, France and Russia, later the US

games.title: True or false: between the wars
items: After the First World War, the US became an international creditor.
Britain and others had borrowed heavily from the US during the war.
In 1914 Henry Ford halved his workers' wages.
He raised the daily wage to $5, roughly doubling it.
Indian exports and imports nearly halved between 1928 and 1934.
World trade collapsed during the Depression and India was hit hard.
During the Depression, the colonial government sharply cut revenue demands on Indian peasants.
Revenue demands were not reduced, which is why peasants suffered so much.
Britain lost much of its Indian cotton market to Japan after the First World War.
During the war British mills were busy with war needs, and Japan stepped into the Indian market.
The First World War was fought only with swords and horses.
It was the first modern industrial war, using machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons.

quiz.q: Which countries formed the Central Powers in the First World War?
quiz.explain: The Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey. Germany, Italy and Japan were the Axis powers of the Second World War.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the First World War sides with the Second World War sides

quiz.q: Why is the First World War called the first modern industrial war?
options: It was the first war fought on horses
It used machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons made by modern industry
It was fought only in factories
It was fought to protect industries in India
quiz.explain: Modern industry supplied weapons on a huge scale, and the war mobilised millions of soldiers.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'industrial' to mean the war was about industry rather than using it

quiz.q: How did the First World War change the US's economic position?
options: The US became the world's biggest debtor
The US lost all its foreign trade
The US became an international creditor
The US was ruled by Britain
quiz.explain: Britain and others borrowed from US banks and the public, so after the war the US was owed more by others than it owed.
quiz.mistake: Reverses debtor and creditor

quiz.q: In 1914, Henry Ford raised his workers' daily wage to how many US dollars?
quiz.explain: Ford raised the daily wage to $5, roughly doubling it, to keep workers on the fast, tiring assembly line. $35 is the price of gold per ounce under Bretton Woods.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Ford's wage with the Bretton Woods gold price

quiz.q: Roughly when did the Great Depression take place?
quiz.explain: The Depression began around 1929 and lasted until the mid-1930s. 1914 to 1918 was the First World War.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Depression with the war years

quiz.q: Which was a cause of the Great Depression?
options: Agricultural overproduction that made farm prices fall
quiz.explain: Too much farm produce pushed prices down, and the fall in US overseas loans spread the crisis to many countries.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a shortage, not a glut, caused falling prices

quiz.q: Between 1928 and 1934, by what percentage did wheat prices fall in India?
quiz.explain: Wheat prices fell by half, cutting peasants' incomes while revenue demands stayed the same.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up this figure with the rinderpest figure of 90 per cent

quiz.q: Which precious metal did India export in large amounts during the Depression?
quiz.explain: Distressed peasants sold gold jewellery, and India exported precious metals, notably gold.
quiz.mistake: Confuses this with the silver that came from Peru centuries earlier

teach.praise: Oh no, prices fell but taxes stayed. Now I see why it hurt so much!
teach.nudge: What caused the Depression, and why were Indian peasants hit hard?

learn.hook: After the Second World War, world leaders met at a hotel in the small town of Bretton Woods, USA, to design new rules for money. Their plan shaped decades of growth.
points: The Second World War (1939 to 1945) was fought between the Axis powers (mainly Germany, Japan and Italy) and the Allies (Britain, France, the Soviet Union and the US). After it, the US emerged as the dominant economic, political and military power.

Economists drew two lessons from the inter-war years: mass production can last only with mass consumption, which needs high and steady incomes and employment; and a country's economic links with the outside world must be managed carefully.

In July 1944 the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference was held at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA. It set up the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to deal with members' external surpluses and deficits, and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank) to finance post-war reconstruction.

The IMF and World Bank, called the Bretton Woods twins, began financial operations in 1947. Under the Bretton Woods system, exchange rates were fixed and the US dollar was anchored to gold at $35 per ounce. The US had an effective veto over key decisions.

Many newly independent developing countries, still facing poverty, joined together as the Group of 77 (G-77) to demand a New International Economic Order (NIEO), seeking real control over their natural resources, fairer prices for raw materials and better access to markets.

example.q: Think it through: Why did newly independent countries form the G-77?
steps: Many former colonies had been held back by long periods of colonial rule.
The IMF and World Bank were dominated by the rich Western countries.
Developing countries felt the system did not serve their needs.
So they joined together to demand a fairer New International Economic Order.
example.answer: They wanted a fairer world economic system, so they organised as the G-77 and demanded an NIEO.

learn.reallife: India is a member of the IMF and the World Bank, and news reports about World Bank loans for Indian projects like roads or clean water continue this post-war story.

quiz.q: Which countries were the main Axis powers in the Second World War?
options: Britain, France and the Soviet Union
quiz.explain: The Axis powers were mainly Germany, Japan and Italy. Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey were the Central Powers of the First World War.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Axis powers with the Central Powers

quiz.q: Where was the conference that set up the IMF and the World Bank held?
quiz.explain: The United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference met at Bretton Woods in July 1944.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with other conferences in the syllabus

quiz.q: In which year was the Bretton Woods conference held?
quiz.explain: It met in July 1944. The IMF and World Bank began operations in 1947.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the conference year with the year operations began

quiz.q: What was the main purpose of the International Monetary Fund?
options: To divide Africa among European powers
To deal with the external surpluses and deficits of member nations
quiz.explain: The IMF dealt with balance of payments problems; financing reconstruction was the World Bank's job.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the roles of the IMF and the World Bank

quiz.q: Which institution was set up to finance post-war reconstruction?
options: The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank)
quiz.explain: The IBRD, popularly called the World Bank, financed rebuilding after the war.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the World Bank with the IMF

quiz.q: Under the Bretton Woods system, the US dollar was fixed to gold at how many US dollars per ounce?
quiz.explain: The dollar was anchored to gold at $35 per ounce, and other currencies were fixed to the dollar.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the gold price with other numbers from the chapter

quiz.q: Which lesson did economists learn from the inter-war experience?
options: Countries should never trade with each other
Farm prices should be allowed to crash
Mass production can be sustained only with mass consumption, needing high and steady incomes
Governments should not care about employment
quiz.explain: The Depression showed that if people lack steady incomes, they cannot buy what factories produce.
quiz.mistake: Draws the opposite lesson from the Depression

quiz.q: What did the G-77 demand?
options: A return to the Corn Laws
The gold standard at $5 an ounce
quiz.explain: The G-77 sought an NIEO giving developing countries real control over their resources and fairer terms of trade.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the purpose of the G-77
